name: Blue Green
lede: Blue green is the color halfway between the two, a deep greenish teal that English builds out of two words because it never had one of its own.

sections.title: Two words for one color
sections.body:
*Blue green* is a compound, not a coinage: it names a color by pointing at its neighbors on either side. The swatch on this page falls in the ISCC-NBS block called strong bluish green, and the German RAL standard has carried a color called blue green (RAL 6004) since 1927 [11]. The xkcd color survey of 2010 also has a blue green, set at the same hex, so the screen value here is a consensus of a few modern sources, not a historical standard [11].

That makes blue green an unusual article. There is no inventor, no dye house, and no first sentence. The history here belongs to the borderland itself: the pigments that sit between green and blue, the old words that did not separate the two, and the eye's own way of treating the pair.

Nearby named colors, each a more specific version of the same borderland, include [[teal]], [[viridian]], [[peacock-blue]], [[sea-green]], [[cobalt-green]] and [[cadet-blue]]. The two parent colors are [[green]] and [[blue]].

sections.title: A border that language drew late
sections.body:
Many languages draw no line here. Ball notes that the Latin word for glass, *vitrum*, stems from a word for a blue-green color, and that the Celtic word *glas* also denotes this hue [1], although in another passage Ball says *glas* ranges from a brownish green to blue [1]. A related puzzle is Caesar's *vitrum*, the substance the Britons used on their bodies: it may mean glass, and what it was is unknown [8].

Ancient Greek was also loose here [5]. Pastoureau explains that *kyaneos*, the source of the modern word cyan, usually names a dark color that might be dark blue, purple, black or brown, and that *glaukos* wavered between green, grey, blue and even yellow [5]. A third word, *chloros*, moved between green and yellow [5]. All three tended to describe paleness or weakness more than a precise shade [5].

In the nineteenth century these oddities fed a myth [5]. The claim was that the Greeks could not see blue, or saw it as dark brown, and Pastoureau's account of the debate is that the idea ran through several decades of scholarship and eventually fell, and he states plainly that recent work on painted architecture and sculpture confirms the Greeks saw colors perfectly well and liked vivid, contrasting hues [5]. The better reading is that a color is rarely named in a society if it plays a minor role in its life, not that it goes unseen [5]. A related claim, that a society's color vocabulary measures its technical advancement, comes from Berlin and Kay's 1969 book and has been contested by many linguists and anthropologists [5].

Elsewhere the borderland has its own single word. In the Chinese five-element scheme the five colors were yellow, red, black, white and a blue-green, each tied to a season, a direction and an element [6].

sections.title: Copper does it
sections.body:
Almost every historical blue green comes from copper. Coles writes that green and blue are both formed from copper ores and that the distinction between the two has often been blurred [7]. Malachite and azurite are cousins in a copper mine, and Finlay reports that Cennino Cennini's palette listed malachite as *verde azzurro*, literally blue-green [8].

The mineral chrysocolla gives a delicate pale blue-green, more translucent in oil than in water-based paint, and was found in wall paintings at Kizil in Turkestan and in tombs of the Twelfth Dynasty in Egypt [7]. Of the gemstones, [[gem:malachite|malachite]] is the banded green one, and [[gem:turquoise|turquoise]] sits closer to the borderland itself [7].

Copper also makes a color when it corrodes. Verdigris forms naturally on copper and bronze exposed to oxygen, water, carbon dioxide or sulfur [6]. Theophrastus gives the earliest known account of making it deliberately, by corroding copper metal with vinegar fumes, in a process like the one for lead white [1]. Coles adds that copper sheets hung over a vinegar bath turn to copper acetate, and that no painter's green was more vivid until the nineteenth century [7].

The names hint at a route. *Verdigris* is French for green from Greece, while the German *Grünspan* means Spanish green, and the sixteenth-century scholar Agricola wrote that the pigment was brought up from Spain [6]. The technique is thought to have traveled west with Arabic alchemy [6]. In the medieval method, copper leaves went into a pot with lye and vinegar or sour wine, were sealed for two weeks, and the green crust was scraped off and powdered [6]. The natural patina is slow: it took thirty years for the Statue of Liberty's copper to turn from pink to green [6].

sections.title: Egyptian blue and the glazed blue-greens
sections.body:
The Egyptians made their own copper blue-green on purpose [6]. The pigment now called [[egyptian-blue]] was first manufactured sometime around 2500 BC [6]. It is calcium copper silicate, made from sand, a copper mineral such as malachite, and chalk or limestone, fired at about 950 to 1000 degrees Celsius and then ground and refired [6]. Depending on how finely it was ground, it ranged from as dark as lapis lazuli to as pale as turquoise [6]. The Romans first called it Egyptian blue; the makers had called it artificial lapis lazuli [6].

Pastoureau adds that Egyptians made splendid objects in blue and blue-green faience, usually funerary pieces such as statuettes, figurines and beads, to which the color was believed to give magical or protective power [4]. St Clair describes one such piece, a blue-green glazed hippopotamus statuette nicknamed William, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art [6].

Manufacture of the pigment faded away, for reasons nobody has settled. St Clair offers two explanations: that demand for blue fell before its twelfth-century revival, and so the secret was not passed down, or that European patrons preferred materials with intrinsic value such as ultramarine [6]. Finds of Egyptian blue in thirteenth-century Italy are believed to be reused old stock [6].

Roman mosaicists used blue and blue-green tesserae freely, and Pastoureau notes that small tesserae allowed subtle blue-green nuances unavailable in wall painting [4].

sections.title: Blue-green in a painting
sections.body:
For painters the problem was permanence. Verdigris is opaque in egg tempera but glassily transparent in oil, so painters mixed it with pine resin to restore its body [6]. It attacked the surface it sat on, discolored, and reacted with other pigments [6]. The greenery in works from Raphael to Tintoretto has withered toward coffee brown [6]. The green dress in Van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait shows the pigment used to spectacular effect [6]. Green cloth was a dyer's problem too: it took two dips, woad then weld, and in some countries dyers caught doing it could face fines or exile [6].

Other greens failed in the opposite direction, toward blue. In Ball's account the yellow component of a mixed green, often a lake glaze over blue underpaint, can lose its hue in light, leaving a sickly blue behind [3]. Pieter Lastman's *Juno Discovering Jupiter with Io* of about 1618 has dark blue-green vegetation, and Jan van Huysum's *Flowers in a Terracotta Vase* of 1736 has patchy blue leaves [3]. The French writer Mérimée had already noticed in 1830 that leaves in several Flemish paintings had turned blue [3].

Where to look: in an old landscape, a tree that has drifted toward a cool blue-green is more likely a fugitive yellow that left than an artist's choice [3].

sections.title: What the eye does with it
sections.body:
Blue-green has a special place in vision. Ball explains that rods, the cells for dim light, absorb most strongly in blue-green light, so objects reflecting those wavelengths, such as leaves, look brighter than red objects at dusk [2]. The Bohemian physiologist J. E. Purkinje first clearly identified this shift in 1825, though artists had noticed it earlier [2].

The color also appears as the answer to red. Albers, Gurney, Westland and Livingstone all report that if you stare at a red for 20 to 30 seconds and look at white, you see its afterimage in blue-green, because tired cones respond less [10]. In the opponent-process picture described by Eckstut, red and green are opposite ends of one channel and blue and yellow of another, so a blue green is easy to imagine, while a reddish green is not [9]. The theory and the trichromatic theory are both treated as compatible and incomplete [9].

The borderland also gave color vocabulary some of its best-loved names: [[aquamarine]], the blue-green of the sea and of the beryl; cadet blue, a grey-greenish blue from military uniforms; and duck egg, a blue-green with a little grey [14].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Blue green is one of the rarer colors in our archive of 23,781 museum paintings [12]. Only 4 hold it within six units of the swatch over at least five per cent of the canvas, about 0.02 per cent, a rarer presence than 77 per cent of the named colors [12]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the pigments that made old blue-greens, verdigris above all, may have changed [12].

The four are an American portrait of 1790, *Dr. Philemon Tracy*, where the color covers 28 per cent of the canvas, Edvard Munch's *Beach* of 1940, Alexej von Jawlensky's *Red Path, St. Prex* of 1915 and Vincent van Gogh's *Green Wheat Fields, Auvers* of 1890 [12]. [[painting:nga-59938|Dr. Philemon Tracy]] is the oldest and the one with the most blue-green, and it is the only match older than 1800 [12]. The Van Gogh match is the smallest, with the color on 9 per cent of the canvas [12]. [[painter:edvard-munch|Munch]] and [[painter:vincent-van-gogh|Van Gogh]] are the two painters in the group [12].

The word is younger than most color words in print. Counts of *blue green* in Google Books rose fastest in the 1920s and peaked in the 1970s [13]. The 1927 date for RAL 6004 falls inside that rise [11][13].
